title: Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy
gist: Chatham House argues the KDP-PUK split, rooted in the collapse of the 2006 Strategic Agreement, has left Iraqi Kurdistan with a caretaker government since 2018 and a de facto two-zone partition, with a PUK devolution plan that would formalize it. With the US military withdrawn at end-September and the US-Iran war distracting Western partners, Turkey, Iran and Baghdad are positioned to exploit the division at the expense of Kurdish autonomy.

insights.claim: Two years after Iraq's Kurdistan Region election, the KDP and PUK still have not formed a government, and a caretaker cabinet originally elected in September 2018 remains in charge.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Prolonged caretaker rule signals policy paralysis in the region, including on oil, gas and trade decisions.

insights.claim: The government-formation deadlock stems from the collapse of the 2006 KDP-PUK Strategic Agreement and the loss of a shared vision for how the region should operate, not from petty disputes over ministerial posts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A structural split will not be solved by a cabinet-seat bargain, so expect the stalemate to persist.
insights.quote: The main impediment to moving forward is not petty disagreements between the two parties over ministerial positions

insights.claim: The Kurdistan Region has effectively split into a KDP zone (Erbil, Duhok) and a PUK zone (Sulaymaniyah, Halabja); security forces and institutions take direction from unelected party leaders rather than KRG ministries.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: De facto partition raises political and counterparty risk for anyone operating across the region.
insights.locator: The KDP is in charge in Erbil

insights.claim: Rents are reportedly extracted from truckers and traders at checkpoints on the border between KDP and PUK areas, indicating the internal divide already taxes trade.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Internal checkpoint rents raise intra-regional trade costs and are an early sign of fiscal fragmentation.

insights.claim: The Kurdistan Parliament has not held a substantive meeting in more than four years; on 6 October KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani publicly urged the parties to reactivate it.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: No functioning legislature means no legal basis for budgets or major reforms.

insights.claim: PUK leaders propose devolving administrative and fiscal authority to governorates, mayors and district directors, citing Switzerland's cantons and the UAE's emirates as models.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch whether this becomes a formal constitutional proposal.

insights.claim: Devolution would formalize each party's existing control over its own governorates, making it the biggest constitutional change in a generation and repudiating the post-civil-war assumption that strong shared institutions are needed for Kurdish autonomy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: It would lock in partition-by-party and reduce any unified negotiating position vis-a-vis Baghdad.

insights.claim: The PUK plan is vague on how revenues would be shared and how oil, gas, electricity and trade decisions would be made, and the KDP opposes it, which is part of why government talks are stalled.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Without answers on energy revenue sharing, the plan raises the risk of competing authorities over Kurdish hydrocarbons.
insights.locator: Many parts of the plan are vague

insights.claim: Many Kurdish voters oppose strengthening the ruling parties without checks and recognize that the PUK plan endangers the region's fragile constitutional position in Iraq.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Public opposition is a constraint on the plan going ahead.

insights.claim: Over the past five years Iraq's federal government has gradually eroded the KRG's ability to manage its political and economic affairs, enabled by KDP-PUK disunity.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Further disunity should extend Baghdad's leverage over Kurdish affairs.

insights.claim: The US completed its military withdrawal from the Kurdistan Region at the end of September after twelve years in the anti-Islamic State coalition, and diplomacy in Erbil has been hampered this year by security concerns from the US-Iran war.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reduced US presence removes a stabilizing referee and security guarantee.
insights.locator: The US presence in the Kurdistan Region

insights.claim: American and European diplomats' failure to bring the KDP and PUK together signals flagging Western influence over top Kurdish leaders, which would worsen if they must deal with empowered local officials answering to party leaders.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Western leverage is likely to keep declining, benefiting regional neighbours.

insights.claim: Turkey and Iran are better placed than the US and Europe to exploit a divided Kurdistan Region because they play a long game through local economic, social and religious ties, and KDP-PUK unity matters little to their calculations.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Disaggregation tends to hand structural advantage to neighbours with local networks.

insights.claim: Turkey's immediate aim is keeping its Kurdish political process, in which the PKK is disarming, on track; the KDP and PUK have backed it and the integration of the Kurdish-led SDF into the new Syrian state, but deeper division could lead Ankara to side with one party and create instability.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The PKK disarmament process is a key variable to monitor for regional stability.

insights.claim: Iran's first goal is keeping Kurdish groups out of its war with the US, and the KDP and PUK are currently in lockstep on avoiding any impression of intervening against Iran.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Near-term Kurdish involvement in the Iran war looks unlikely.

insights.claim: Iran also wants its own Kurdish armed groups curtailed, even expelled from Iraqi Kurdistan; weak, divided KRG institutions make that hard, making unilateral Iranian action more likely.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Raises the risk of Iranian strikes or pressure in the Kurdistan Region.

insights.claim: Without a US security presence, regional interference could push Baghdad to become more hands-on in Kurdistan Region affairs, which would harm Kurdish self-governance and inflame KDP-PUK tensions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A feedback loop of outside interference and internal rivalry points to greater Baghdad control.
insights.locator: In the absence of a US security presence

insights.claim: Continued KDP-PUK impasse risks irreversible decline of the frameworks that have enabled Kurdish self-governance for two decades, leaving the region for other actors to pick apart.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Autonomy erosion could become hard to reverse, so decisions made soon matter.
insights.quote: Otherwise, it risks becoming a place that other actors pick apart at the expense of Kurdish autonomy.
